For GPT-6-Astra, FC rises from 50.79% to 94.40% with explicit requirements, reaching 97.45% when evidence is additionally requested. Claude and Gemini show the same aggregate pattern. Correct-label responses that fail the content checks become rare for Astra, disappear for Gemini in both explicit conditions, and decrease sharply for Claude. Thus, the original separation between Accuracy and FC is highly sensitive to how the required response is described. All Astra responses are already parseable in every condition, and parsing failures are rare for Claude and Gemini. A parseable response can still omit a required action, underspecify a clarification question, or fail to express an accepted repair. Explicit requirements address this broader mismatch between choosing the warranted category and supplying its required content. H2 applies the same core acceptance checks in every condition (Appendix F ). 5.3 Judgment Also Changes, but Not Equally Across Sources The benefit extends beyond expressing a decision that was already correct. Across all three models, both Accuracy and IFC improve with explicit requirements and improve further in aggregate when evidence is requested (Table 1 ). Response specification therefore affects which next step is selected, not only whether the accompanying content is accepted. The evidence condition has the strongest aggregate results. Witness validity is assessed separately in Appendix E . The effects vary by source. Explicit JSON improves Astra’s preference decisions but lowers its constraint Accuracy; adding evidence then improves constraint decisions while slightly reducing preference Accuracy. Claude’s constraint Accuracy instead increases with explicit JSON and then decreases slightly with evidence. The direction of these source-level changes differs across models. The earlier OSS comparison also reports a different decision trend on its separate collection (Appendix H ). Response requirements affect intervention decisions, with source-dependent gains and reversals. 5.4 Separating Answer Generation from Intervention Reminders We use two complementary comparisons to examine answer construction and intervention emphasis. Both use the same 1,080 tasks for Astra, Claude, and Gemini: five complete six-task groups per cell, sampled without consulting model answers or scores. The selection comparison presents four candidate responses, including exactly one fully correct candidate, and uses each model’s existing same-task H2 explicit-JSON generation responses as its baseline. The wording comparison instead collects new responses under neutral wording and an intervention reminder, retaining identical task facts and explicit JSON requirements. Appendix K provides the construction, record checks, and detailed results. Supplying candidate answers does not uniformly improve intervention decisions (Table 2 ). Astra and Gemini improve in aggregate, whereas Claude deteriorates. All three models improve on constraint FC, but this common benefit does not extend uniformly to the other sources. For Claude, preference and objective performance decline, and unnecessary interventions nearly double. The selection condition changes answer construction and supplies both correct answer content and distractors. Intervention reminders yield only modest incremental gains once the response requirements are already explicit (Figure 5 ). Unnecessary interventions decrease slightly for all three models, while missed interventions decrease for Claude and remain unchanged for Astra and Gemini. Paired comparisons contain both improvements and reversals. These effects measure the addition of an intervention reminder to explicit content requirements. Taken together, the comparisons show that specifying response content, providing candidate answers, and emphasizing intervention availability produce distinct behavioral effects rather than interchangeable improvements. Exact scores and counts are in Table 38 . 6 Conclusion We introduced actionable indeterminacy to distinguish uncertainty that can remain unresolved from obstacles that require clarification or constraint repair before action. Our solver-grounded benchmark makes this distinction testable through matched action/intervention pairs across four decision structures. Under the original prompts, models can recognize necessary interventions yet still intervene when action is already justified. Crucially, response requirements shape both the decisions models make and whether their accompanying content is accepted. Making the required content explicit substantially improves fully correct responses and can change intervention decisions even when outputs are already parseable, although gains vary across models and sources. These findings support evaluating decision correctness, matched-pair reliability, and response-content validity separately.
